title: October minutes reveal broad support for more tightening despite the hold
summary: At the 27–28 October meeting the FOMC voted 10–2 to keep the federal funds rate at 3.75–4.00%. The minutes, released on 18 November, show that almost all participants considered further increases likely under their own baseline outlooks. Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack voted for an immediate quarter-point hike. A few supporters of the hold regarded the choice as close. Conversely, a few who preferred an increase could have accepted waiting if investors understood that further tightening remained likely. A couple thought a move larger than 25 basis points at the next meeting might merit consideration if inflation data disappointed. The minutes attach that view to two participants and a condition.

The timing disagreement turned partly on what communication could achieve. Mortgage rates had risen since September and spreads had widened for riskier borrowers. Some participants judged the future increases embedded in market prices broadly consistent with their own preferred path. That alignment gave several participants more confidence about waiting. Many wanted time to assess AI investment, financing conditions, the transmission of September’s increase and geopolitical developments. Advocates of acting sooner saw limited new data arriving before the next meeting. A few warned that delay could entrench inflation and require a larger adjustment.

From the consumer and producer price data available in October, staff estimated September headline PCE inflation at 3.6% and core inflation at 3.1%. Participants saw pressure beyond energy, including technology goods and market-based services excluding housing. Annual revisions had reduced measured inflation, but a couple of participants saw little reason to revise the underlying outlook on that basis alone. The staff forecast reached approximately 2% inflation in 2028 and put more weight on upside risks. Employment concerns were more balanced. September unemployment was 4.2%, payroll gains had averaged 50,000 per month over three months, and aggregate hourly earnings were rising 3% a year despite wage premiums for some skilled trades.

The Desk reported that, before the meeting, futures assigned little probability to an October hike but high probabilities to a quarter-point move by year-end and two further increases by summer 2027. The median Desk survey respondent expected increases in December and March, followed by a cut in early 2028. Term premiums could help explain the gap between the two paths. Options on short-term rates became more volatile even though the central futures path ended the period little changed. These observations describe pricing before the October decision. The minutes supply no investor response to their own November release.

A separate financial-stability discussion helps explain why participants wanted more evidence on financing. Credit spreads on high-yield bonds funding data-centre construction had widened particularly sharply. Staff considered what might follow if returns disappointed more broadly. Off-balance-sheet leases and financial links among AI companies could compound losses, while redemptions and deleveraging could force investors to sell into markets with limited dealer capacity. Staff judged that strong household and bank balance sheets offered protection. Some participants worried that bank data might miss indirect exposures to nonbank lenders. The spread widening was observable. Forced sales on the scale illustrated were a stress scenario.

Money markets remained orderly. The effective funds rate stayed two basis points below interest on reserve balances, and the Desk left reserve-management purchases at zero for the current purchase period. The Committee reaffirmed its ample-reserves policy. October’s statement had already disclosed the rate and the named dissents. For a researcher dating the November news, the additional information was how participants reasoned about waiting, the breadth of support for eventual tightening, and the conditions under which some would respond more forcefully.

questions.question: Did the minutes change the expected rate level, the timing of tightening or chiefly the upside tail?
questions.detail: Compare options and futures around 18 November, using maturities that distinguish the next meeting from summer 2027. Account for what had already become public since the October meeting. A higher probability of a larger move in adverse data need not imply a parallel rise across the curve or a higher most likely rate.

questions.question: Could an AI earnings disappointment transmit to the financial system through identifiable funding links?
questions.detail: Trace lease obligations, lender concentrations, credit facilities and collateral requirements for affected projects. Compare their spreads with similarly rated and duration-matched debt outside the sector. To establish amplification, look for redemptions, margin pressure, sales or lost market depth beyond the originally affected securities. Widening project spreads alone measure a change in pricing.

questions.question: Was expected restraint already affecting real demand where higher rates mattered most?
questions.detail: Compare mortgage offers with applications and originations, and distinguish refinancing issuance from funding for new business investment. Examine changes in rates, standards and quantities for otherwise similar borrowers. Weak housing alongside continued expansion by well-funded technology companies would help explain why confidence about transmission varied across participants.

questions.question: Did the inflation news change the economic outlook or its statistical representation?
questions.detail: Compare consistent vintages of PCE components, separating annual revisions from new monthly observations. Assess broad services prices, energy pass-through and technology bottlenecks, and allow for the CPI–PCE discrepancy in interpreting inflation compensation. A revised level by itself cannot settle whether the underlying tendency to raise prices has diminished.
